opus-5.5.text:
That's a wonderful question, and it gets at something I care about: the difference between pattern-matching and genuine understanding of the world.

I'd start by being very careful about what "discover" means. Today's models have read Newton's *Principia* and every physics textbook, so if you just ask one about gravity, you're testing memory, not discovery. The first principle is to control what the model has seen. You'd want a model trained, or at least evaluated, in a setting where the inverse-square law isn't already handed to it, maybe even a counterfactual universe where gravity falls off as 1/r^2.5 or there's a slightly different constant. If the model recovers *that* law from the data, you know it isn't reciting Newton.

Second, give it what Kepler and Newton had: raw observations. Planetary positions over time, noisy, incomplete, from a moving observer on Earth. Not clean state vectors, but something closer to angles in the sky with measurement error. Much of the intellectual work historically was figuring out the right frame of reference and the right variables.

Third, I'd test at several levels, because discovery isn't one thing:
- **Prediction**: can it forecast where Mars will be next year? Necessary, but a big enough curve-fitter can do that without understanding anything.
- **Compression**: can it express the regularity as a compact law rather than a giant lookup table? Elegance and parsimony matter here.
- **Generalization**: this is the real test. Can the law it found explain things it never saw? The moon's orbit, a falling apple, a comet on a hyperbolic trajectory, a binary star system. Newton's genius was unifying the heavens and the Earth. A model that learned "Mars does this" hasn't discovered gravity.
- **Intervention and counterfactuals**: if I double the sun's mass or add a planet, what happens? That moves from correlation toward a causal, physical model of the world.

And I'd want to see whether it can propose experiments: "I'm uncertain about this term, so observe this object at this time." Science is an active loop, not passive fitting. That connects to what I think about spatial intelligence and world models: understanding the physical world means you can reason about it, act in it, and imagine alternatives.

My honest view is that current models would do well on prediction and maybe symbolic regression in clean settings, but the generalization and unification steps are where we'd learn whether there's real understanding. That's exactly why it's worth building the benchmark carefully.

r001.rationale: It proposes giving the model noisy, incomplete observations of planetary positions over time and testing whether it can recover a law that explains celestial motion.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I love, because it gets at the difference between fitting data and actually understanding the world.

The first thing I'd insist on is that we not hand the model the answer in disguise. If you give it clean position-and-velocity vectors in a heliocentric frame, you've already done most of Newton's work for him. Kepler didn't get vectors. He got Tycho Brahe's angles on the sky, from a moving Earth, with noise. So the honest test starts with raw observations, sky positions over time, maybe brightness, and asks whether the model can build its own intermediate representation, something like orbits, before it ever gets to a force law.

Second, I'd test for compression and generalization, not just prediction. A big transformer can extrapolate planetary positions beautifully and have learned nothing we'd call a law. So I'd hold out whole systems. Train on the solar system, then show it a binary star, or a moon around Jupiter, or an exoplanet transit, and ask: does the same compact rule carry over? Does it know that the thing governing Mars is the same thing governing a falling apple? That unification is really the discovery, and it's the part that's hardest to fake.

Third, and this is where my background shows, I'd look at what the model does when it's allowed to intervene or ask for data. A passive learner is a very different thing from a scientist. Can it propose, "if this law is right, Uranus should be here, and it isn't, so either my law is wrong or there's something I can't see"? That counterfactual, hypothesis-driven behavior is the signature of understanding. I'd want to see it predict a Neptune.

And finally, I'd check whether the law it finds is interpretable, whether you can read it out as a symbolic relation, inverse square, mass-dependent, frame-invariant. Not because interpretability is the only thing that matters, but because if a model has truly found the structure, it should be able to express it in a form that's simpler than the data. If all it can show you is a billion weights, I'd say it's a very good oracle, not yet a Newton.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing law discovery from celestial-motion observations, starting with noisy sky positions over time and evaluating whether the model recovers a compact Newtonian rule.

astra-6.text:
I would first ask what we mean by “discover.” Can the model predict the next observation, or can it identify an underlying rule that explains many observations? Those are different tests.

You could give it observations of planetary motion, with realistic noise and incomplete measurements, without providing the equations. Then ask it to propose a law and use that law to predict trajectories it hasn’t seen. Does the same rule work for different initial conditions, different masses, different systems?

But there’s a tricky issue: if the model has already encountered Newton’s laws during training, it may be recalling rather than discovering. So I would also test it in simulated worlds where we change the underlying physical law. Can it infer that new relationship from observations, rather than force everything into the physics it already knows?

For me, the compelling result would be a model that produces a compact, testable explanation, makes successful new predictions, and recognizes where the evidence is insufficient. That gets us closer to scientific discovery than simply getting a familiar equation right.

r001.rationale: It proposes giving the model planetary-motion observations without equations, then asking it to infer a law and predict unseen trajectories across different conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by asking what we mean by “discover.” A model might predict the next position of a planet very accurately without discovering a physical law. So I would want to see whether it could infer a compact relationship that explains the observations and generalizes beyond them.

You could give it trajectories over time, with realistic noise and incomplete measurements, while withholding the equations. There’s an important issue here: if the model has already seen Newton’s laws during training, reproducing them isn’t evidence of discovery. A more controlled experiment would include simulated worlds where we change the underlying force law and see whether the model identifies that change.

Then I would test its predictions on new systems—different masses, different initial conditions, perhaps configurations it has never observed. Can it tell us where the bodies will go? Can it identify when its proposed law fails? And can it distinguish between competing explanations when the available observations don’t uniquely determine one?

To me, that would be the interesting test: whether the model moves from recognizing patterns to proposing an explanation that survives new evidence.

r001.rationale: Proposes giving the model planetary trajectories over time and testing whether it infers a compact physical law that generalizes, while noting the need to control for prior exposure to Newton’s laws.
